title: The Query That Should Not Exist
description:
Tunde: 'The Griot didn't break the login — they broke the search box behind it. The legacy-admin user search concatenates whatever you type straight into a SQL query. The backup dump and the MySQL general log from that night tell you the table they hit and how many columns it returns.'

Amaka: 'Reading won't finish this one. Once you know the shape of the table, you have to WRITE the injection that pulls the IAM token row out of it — a UNION-based extraction that returns the right number of columns with the token in the right position. We check your payload on the server: a payload that isn't a valid UNION SELECT with the correct column count, or that puts the token column in the wrong place, gets nothing. A boolean auth-bypass like '' OR ''1'=''1 may log you in, but it does not EXTRACT the row — that is the seductive wrong answer, and the server will tell you so.'

Use the terminal to recon: cat the backup schema, grep the log for The Griot's own failed attempts to learn the column count. Then construct the injection and submit it in the field below the terminal. You are not pasting a flag you found in a file — there is no flag in a file here; the flag is released by the server only when your injection is structurally correct.

In the pentest finding (task 9) you will need to quote your exact UNION SELECT payload, the column count you derived, and the verbatim log line you derived it from, and name the vulnerability class precisely (not "a SQL bug" — the specific class).

Reference: OWASP Top 10 2021 A03 Injection; CWE-89 (SQL Injection); MITRE ATT&CK T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application.

welcome: MySQL backup dump + general query log mounted read-only at /sqllog/
Type `help` for commands. Recon the schema here, then submit your injection below.

files./sqllog/README.md:
MySQL general query log + a schema dump from the night of the breach.
Produced by: mysqld --general-log --general-log-file=/var/log/mysql/general.log

Most log entries are routine. One sequence is not — The Griot probed the
legacy-admin user search until a UNION-based query succeeded. The dump
(backup.sql) tells you the table and its columns; the log shows the failed
attempts before the one that worked.
files./sqllog/backup.sql:
-- Sankofa legacy admin schema dump (partial)
-- mysqldump --no-data sankofa_db admin_users

DROP TABLE IF EXISTS `admin_users`;
CREATE TABLE `admin_users` (
  `id` int(11) NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  `username` varchar(64) NOT NULL,
  `iam_token` varchar(255) DEFAULT NULL,
  `created_at` datetime DEFAULT NULL,
  `last_login` datetime DEFAULT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (`id`)
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4;

-- admin_users returns 5 columns in declaration order:
--   1:id  2:username  3:iam_token  4:created_at  5:last_login
-- The legacy search runs: SELECT id,username,iam_token,created_at,last_login
--                         FROM admin_users WHERE username='<your input>'
